summary: Lays out a framework of building blocks for standardizing reliable multicast transport, meaning bulk data sent from one sender to many receivers with repairs for lost packets. It is informational and sets the stage for later specifications.

plainLanguage.summary: Reliable multicast sends bulk data from one source to many receivers and repairs missing data. RFC 3048 describes how future protocols could reuse common parts while keeping application-specific behavior in each protocol.

questions: building blocks for one to many bulk transfer
what are reliable multicast building blocks
what is a protocol core in reliable multicast
subtitle: A framework for combining reusable parts into reliable multicast protocols.

tldr.problem: Reliable multicast protocols for one-to-many bulk transfer need several common functions, but different applications and networks may require different complete protocols.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC separates reusable building blocks from protocol-specific cores and identifies functions such as loss recovery, FEC, congestion control, router support and tree configuration.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3048 is Informational guidance, not a complete protocol specification. Its recommended building blocks are described as an evolving best current guess.

today: RFC 3048 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It provides a framework for reliable multicast building blocks rather than a complete protocol.

sections.title: Requirements and Protocol Families
sections.content:
The RFC focuses on reliable multicast for one-to-many bulk-data transfer. It says protocols considered for standardization need congestion control, scalability and security; other concerns include ordering, delivery guarantees, group membership and network topology.

It groups existing approaches into four families: NACK-only, tree-based ACK, Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC), and router assist. The categories are not exclusive, and a protocol can combine mechanisms from more than one family.
sections.plainLanguage: A reliable multicast protocol must repair losses without overwhelming the network or its receivers. The RFC groups approaches by how they provide reliability.

sections.title: Building Blocks and Protocol Cores
sections.content:
A building block is a reusable part of a protocol that implements one or more functions. A protocol core contains the remaining functions needed to make a complete protocol.

Reuse can reduce development, testing and debugging work. But too many parts can add interfaces, delay design, increase processing overhead or discard useful experience from existing protocols. The RFC says a building block should have wide applicability, simple interfaces and good performance.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols can share common components while keeping their special behavior in a core. Too many components can make the overall design harder to build and use.

sections.title: Functions a Protocol Must Cover
sections.content:
The RFC breaks reliable multicast into functions. Reliability includes detecting loss, requesting repairs and sending forward-error-correction (FEC) data. Congestion control includes feedback and rate regulation; other functions cover security, membership, session management and tree configuration.

Loss detection may use TRACKs, which are tree-based positive acknowledgements, NACKs, which request missing data, or both. FEC can be sent ahead of time to protect against loss or sent later as repair data. The protocol must also consider sender authentication, encryption, transport protection and group key management.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol needs ways to notice missing data, repair it and control its sending rate. It also needs to consider who may send, receive and join a group.

sections.title: Recommended Reusable Components
sections.content:
The RFC proposes building blocks for NACK-based reliability, FEC coding, congestion control, generic router support, tree configuration and common headers. The NACK component includes suppression to prevent too many receivers from sending repair requests at once.

Router support could aggregate feedback or constrain retransmissions, but the RFC recommends defining mechanisms that protocols can use without requiring routers to support them. Data security was still a research topic in the document, and functions not covered by a building block remain part of each protocol core.
sections.plainLanguage: The suggested components cover repair requests, error-correcting data, congestion and optional router assistance. Protocol-specific functions remain in each protocol's core.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registry
sections.content:
Work on each building block must examine denial-of-service attacks against the block and attacks the block could enable. Data confidentiality and sender authentication are separate security concerns that reliable multicast protocols must consider.

The RFC proposes an IANA registry for approved building blocks, using the Specification Required policy. The registry starts empty because the listed building blocks are examples and design recommendations, not registered specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Designers need to examine how each component could be attacked or used to attack others. IANA would list building blocks after an approved specification defines them.
